**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on Q3 compute capacity decision

**Summary**

We are at a decision point on AI compute. Our current cluster of eight GPUs is running at roughly 55% average utilisation, while our inference backlog is growing and our training experiments are queuing behind each other. The vendor quote for four additional units arrived last week, and it is tempting to treat the purchase as the obvious answer. After two weeks of analysis, our recommendation is the opposite: we should spend the next quarter improving utilisation of the hardware we already own, and defer the purchase decision until we have evidence we genuinely need it.

**The case against buying now**

The financial argument is straightforward. The quoted price for four units, including networking, racks, and the power provisioning our facilities team says we would need, comes to a figure that would consume most of our remaining annual capital budget. That is money we cannot spend on anything else for the rest of the year. The opportunity cost is real: the same budget would fund two additional engineers, or a managed inference contract that would let us scale serving without owning the capacity at all.

More important than cost is reversibility. Hardware we buy is hardware we own. GPU resale values are notoriously volatile, and our own history with the last expansion — two units that sat underused for eight months before we repurposed them for batch jobs — suggests our demand forecasts are not reliable enough to justify irreversible capital commitments. If our workload mix shifts, as it did when the product team moved from fine-tuning to API-based models last year, owned capacity becomes a liability rather than an asset. Utilisation improvements, by contrast, are almost entirely reversible: better scheduling, batching, and model optimisation cost engineering time, which flexes with our priorities.

**The case for utilisation first**

Fifty-five percent utilisation means nearly half of our paid capacity is idle on average. Some of that idle time is structural — overnight lulls, weekend dips — but a meaningful portion is self-inflicted. Our serving stack processes requests one at a time when dynamic batching could consolidate them, and our internal benchmarks suggest batching alone could lift serving throughput by 30 to 40%. Our training jobs are scheduled manually, which leads to fragmentation: a job needing two GPUs will not start when two single GPUs are free, because nothing reslices the cluster. A proper scheduler would fix that. Finally, our models have not been quantised or distilled since the spring; the inference team believes a quantised variant could serve the same traffic on roughly 60% of the current GPU-hours with acceptable latency.

If all three initiatives land, we estimate effective capacity rises by 50% or more — approaching, though not fully matching, what the new hardware would provide. But the comparison is not apples to apples, and that is where honest uncertainty matters. Utilisation gains do not help with peak load. Our traffic spikes on weekday mornings, and if peak demand already saturates the cluster, better average utilisation does nothing for the users who experience latency degradation at 9 a.m. We have not yet measured whether our latency SLO violations correlate with saturation or with something else entirely, and we should find out before spending on either path.

**Reliability considerations**

There is also a reliability argument that cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy: a single failed unit today removes 12.5% of our capacity, and our maintenance windows are constrained because we cannot easily absorb the loss. Buying more would ease that. But better utilisation practices — checkpointing, queue-based scheduling, graceful degradation to smaller models — improve resilience without adding physical complexity, and they are practices we will need regardless of how much hardware we eventually own.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next quarter on the utilisation programme: dynamic batching, cluster scheduling, and model quantisation, in roughly that order of expected impact. Instrument latency against saturation so that by quarter's end we have real data on whether peak capacity, not average utilisation, is the binding constraint. If it is, the purchase case becomes much stronger and we can make it with evidence rather than anxiety. If it is not, we will have bought ourselves capacity through engineering rather than capital, and kept our options open.

The risk of this path is that we spend a quarter optimising and still end up buying hardware, having delayed relief for the team. We accept that risk. The alternative — buying first and optimising never — is the more common failure mode, and the more expensive one.

We are happy to walk through the numbers in detail at Thursday's planning session.

**MEMO: To — Platform Engineering Team | From — Infrastructure Working Group | Re — GPU capacity: buy or optimize?**

Over the past few weeks we've been circling a question that keeps coming up in standups: do we buy more local AI hardware, or do we get more out of what we already own? I want to lay out how I see the trade-offs, because I think the framing matters as much as the answer, and then make a recommendation we can act on this quarter.

The case for buying more hardware is the obvious one. Our inference queue times spike during business hours, the batch jobs we want to run overnight are competing with interactive workloads, and every engineer who has waited forty minutes for a fine-tuning run knows the frustration. On paper, adding capacity makes the pain go away. But the paper is expensive. Current-generation accelerators at the spec we'd want run well into six figures for a meaningful node, and that's before networking, power, cooling, and the rack space we'd need to find. More importantly, that capital is committed. Once the purchase order is signed, the money is spent regardless of whether our workload mix changes, and our workload mix has changed twice in the last year already. There's also a hidden cost people rarely put in the spreadsheet: the operational burden. Every additional node is something we patch, monitor, and eventually decommission. A team our size feels that.

The case for improving utilisation is less glamorous but, I think, stronger. When we actually instrumented the fleet, the numbers were humbling. Our headline utilisation figure looked respectable, but it was inflated by low-priority jobs parked on GPUs around the clock. The interactive workloads that actually drive our latency complaints were getting a fraction of the capacity, and the scheduling between them was essentially first-come, first-served. That means a meaningful share of our capacity problem isn't a capacity problem at all — it's an allocation problem. Fixing it means better queueing discipline, real priority classes, batching small inference requests, and moving our periodic training runs into windows when interactive demand is low. None of that is free: it's engineering time, probably two to three people for a quarter, and it introduces some risk while we shake out the scheduler. But the cost is measured in salaries we're already paying, not new capital, and — crucially — it's reversible. If we build better scheduling and it turns out we were wrong about the headroom, we've lost a quarter of effort and gained permanent operational skill. If we buy hardware and it turns out we were wrong, we've lost a very large amount of money and own machines we can't easily resell at anything close to what we paid.

Latency deserves its own note, because it's the argument I hear most often for buying. It's true that more hardware is the fastest way to cut tail latencies, and some of our latency targets are genuinely hard commitments. But most of our p99 spikes trace back to contention, not raw throughput — jobs queuing behind each other, memory thrashing when a large model evicts a small one. Contention is exactly what utilisation work fixes. I'd expect the first round of scheduling improvements to deliver most of the latency relief we'd get from new hardware, at a fraction of the cost, and we can verify that within weeks rather than after a procurement cycle.

Reliability cuts both ways. More nodes give us redundancy, but they also give us more components that fail and more surface area to operate. Right now a single node failure takes out a visible chunk of our capacity, and that's a real argument for eventually having more hardware. But redundancy bought before you understand your actual demand profile tends to be redundancy in the wrong places. Better utilisation work includes failover and preemption policies that improve reliability today, with the hardware we have.

So my recommendation: commit this quarter to the utilisation track. Fund the scheduling and batching work properly, set explicit targets — p99 latency, GPU-hours of useful work, queue wait — and review them in ninety days. If we hit those targets, we've likely deferred or eliminated a purchase. If we fall short, we'll be in a far better position to specify exactly what hardware we need and to justify it with real data rather than frustration. That's the other benefit of this path: it converts an uncertain decision into a better-informed one.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. Our instrumentation is young, and it's possible the numbers understate true demand, particularly if the roadmap adds model families we haven't planned for. If that happens, buying becomes right quickly, and we shouldn't let sunk effort in the utilisation track stop us. The point of the ninety-day review is to keep that option open, not to foreclose it. Buying is not off the table; it's on hold until the evidence justifies it.

Happy to walk through the utilisation data with anyone who wants the detail. Comments welcome before Friday's planning session.

**MEMO: Local AI Hardware — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** Capacity strategy for our on-premise inference fleet
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past month we've been debating a question that keeps resurfacing: should we purchase additional GPU hardware for our local inference workloads, or should we invest in squeezing more out of the machines we already own? I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because I believe the framing matters more than the immediate dollar figures.

Let's start with the obvious temptation. Our utilization dashboards look uncomfortable. Peak-hour saturation on the two A100 nodes regularly exceeds 90 percent, and queue times during the morning window have crept from seconds to minutes. The instinctive response is to buy our way out of the problem. Hardware is a known quantity: we issue a purchase order, racks arrive, capacity goes up, dashboards turn green. There's real appeal in that certainty, and I don't want to dismiss it. Latency is a product feature for us — our internal users have built workflows that assume sub-second responses, and every minute of queueing erodes trust in the platform. If we degrade that experience further, we risk teams quietly migrating to external APIs, which would fragment our data handling and undermine the compliance posture that motivated local deployment in the first place.

But buying hardware is the most expensive and least reversible option on the table. Capital expenditure on accelerators is lumpy — a meaningful fraction of our annual budget in one stroke — and it commits us to a depreciation schedule regardless of whether demand materializes as forecast. Our own demand history is instructive here: two quarters ago we projected sustained growth that flattened after the reorg, and the capacity we provisioned for it sat largely idle. GPUs also depreciate quickly in both financial and capability terms; the card that looks like a sound investment today may be awkwardly outclassed in eighteen months. Once purchased, this hardware is difficult to redeploy or resell without meaningful loss. That irreversibility deserves weight.

The alternative — improving utilization — has a very different cost and risk profile. Our profiling work suggests we're leaving 25 to 40 percent of effective throughput on the table. Batch sizes are conservative because we never tuned them after the model migration. Several long-running batch jobs run during business hours and compete with interactive traffic; shifting them to overnight windows is a scheduling change, not an engineering project. We haven't implemented dynamic batching or continuous batching on the serving layer, and our quantization story is inconsistent across models. None of this is glamorous, but it is cheap, fast, and — critically — reversible. If we tune batching and it doesn't deliver, we've lost a few engineer-weeks. If it does deliver, we've bought ourselves six to twelve months of headroom at a fraction of the cost of new silicon, and we'll have learned things about our own workload that make any future purchase smarter.

There's also the opportunity cost of the purchase path to consider. The engineering time required to integrate, benchmark, and rebalance workloads across new nodes is not trivial, and it would come largely from the same people who would be doing the utilization work. Money spent on hardware is money not spent on the observability improvements and serving-layer work that will pay off regardless of how much metal we own.

That said, I want to be honest about the uncertainty. Utilization gains are estimates, not guarantees. Our profiling may overstate recoverable capacity, and demand could grow faster than we expect — a new product launch or an expanded internal base could overwhelm even a well-tuned fleet. If that happens, we will need to buy hardware, and possibly quickly. The good news is that these paths are not mutually exclusive; they're sequenced. Utilization work is the cheap option we exercise first, and it doesn't foreclose the purchase option — it just defers it until we know our real requirement rather than our panicked one.

So my recommendation is this: commit the next quarter to a focused utilization program — dynamic batching, workload scheduling, quantization where quality permits, and better capacity observability — with a defined checkpoint at the end of the quarter. If projected peak utilization still exceeds 80 percent at that point, we proceed with a hardware purchase, sized against the data we'll then have. This keeps our options open, spends the cheap money before the expensive money, and ensures that when we do buy, we're buying from a position of understanding rather than urgency.

I'd welcome pushback, particularly from anyone closer to the latency-sensitive workloads. Let's discuss Thursday.

— Infra Working Group
